title: Compare Internet Connection Types, Network Types, and Their Characteristics

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Internet services reach customers through different media, while network types describe a network's geographic scale, connection style, or specialized purpose.
For this objective, compare satellite, fiber, cable, DSL, cellular, and WISP connections, then recognize LAN, WAN, PAN, MAN, SAN, and WLAN.
sections.callout: Internet connection → how service arrives. Network type → what area or purpose the network serves.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: When a scenario describes the medium used for internet access or the size and purpose of a network, can you identify the correct connection or network type?

sections.title: Internet Connection Types
paragraphs: Internet providers deliver connectivity through different transmission media and infrastructure. Availability, distance, performance, latency, environmental limits, and deployment requirements vary by connection type.
sections.callout: No single connection is best everywhere; identify the medium and scenario.

sections.title: Satellite
paragraphs: Satellite internet uses satellites and customer equipment such as a dish or terminal. It can serve rural or remote locations where terrestrial broadband is unavailable.
Considerations include latency, weather, equipment, line of sight, availability, and capacity. Low-Earth-orbit systems can offer lower latency than traditional geostationary service.
sections.callout: Remote location plus satellite equipment → satellite internet.

sections.title: Fiber
paragraphs: Fiber internet transmits data as light through fiber-optic cable. It can provide very high bandwidth, low latency, long-distance transmission, strong upload performance, and resistance to electromagnetic interference.
At the customer premises, fiber service may terminate at an Optical Network Terminal (ONT).
sections.callout: Optical cabling, light, high bandwidth, and low latency → fiber.

sections.title: Cable
paragraphs: Cable internet commonly uses coaxial infrastructure associated with cable television networks. It can provide high-speed broadband, though shared provider segments can make local utilization affect performance.
sections.callout: Internet arrives over coaxial cable → cable service.

sections.title: Digital Subscriber Line (DSL)
paragraphs: Digital Subscriber Line (DSL) carries broadband over traditional telephone copper wiring. Performance depends on the DSL technology, copper quality, and distance from provider equipment.
sections.callout: Broadband over telephone copper → DSL.

sections.title: Cable vs. DSL
sections.callout: Coax = cable; phone line = DSL.

sections.title: Fiber vs. Cable vs. DSL
sections.callout: Light → fiber; coax → cable; phone copper → DSL.

sections.title: Cellular Internet
paragraphs: Cellular internet uses a mobile carrier network such as 4G or 5G. Smartphones, tablets, hotspots, cellular laptops, and cellular routers can use it.
Performance depends on coverage, signal strength, congestion, carrier infrastructure, and device capabilities.
sections.callout: Cell towers plus mobile carrier → cellular internet.

sections.title: Wireless Internet Service Provider (WISP)
paragraphs: A Wireless Internet Service Provider (WISP) supplies internet through wireless links instead of running a wired connection all the way to the customer. Fixed customer equipment often communicates with a provider tower or access point.
sections.callout: Rooftop receiver aimed at a local ISP tower → WISP.

sections.title: Cellular vs. WISP

table.caption: Wireless internet service models
rows: Often-fixed customer equipment linked to wireless ISP infrastructure

sections.callout: Cellular = mobile carrier; WISP = fixed wireless ISP.

sections.title: Satellite vs. WISP

table.caption: Rural wireless infrastructure
rows: Terrestrial provider tower or access point

sections.callout: Sky → satellite; tower → WISP.

sections.title: Internet Connection Recognition Map
bullets: Satellite → satellite communication and remote coverage
sections.callout: The strongest clue is usually the medium or provider infrastructure.

sections.title: Network Types
paragraphs: Network types are classified by geographic size, connection method, or purpose. Objective 2.7 includes LAN, WAN, PAN, MAN, SAN, and WLAN.
sections.callout: Ask: what kind of network is this?

sections.title: Local Area Network (LAN)
paragraphs: A Local Area Network (LAN) connects computers, servers, printers, switches, and other devices within a limited area such as a home, office, school building, or small business.
sections.callout: Devices connected within one office or local site → LAN.

sections.title: Wide Area Network (WAN)
paragraphs: A Wide Area Network (WAN) spans a broad geographic area and can connect multiple LANs across cities or regions. The internet is the largest familiar example.
sections.callout: Company connects offices across distant cities → WAN.

sections.title: LAN vs. WAN
sections.callout: LAN = building; WAN = beyond the building.

sections.title: Personal Area Network (PAN)
paragraphs: A Personal Area Network (PAN) connects devices in the small area around one person. A phone linked to a smartwatch and wireless earbuds is a common example.
sections.callout: Nearby personal devices → PAN.

sections.title: PAN vs. LAN

table.caption: Personal and local scope
rows: A home, office, or local site

sections.callout: PAN = person; LAN = location.

sections.title: Metropolitan Area Network (MAN)
paragraphs: A Metropolitan Area Network (MAN) is larger than a typical LAN but smaller than a traditional WAN, commonly covering a city, metropolitan area, or collection of nearby sites.
sections.callout: Network connects locations across a city → MAN.

sections.title: LAN vs. MAN vs. WAN
sections.callout: Local → metro → wide.

sections.title: Storage Area Network (SAN)
paragraphs: A Storage Area Network (SAN) is a specialized network that provides servers high-performance access to shared storage arrays and enterprise storage resources.
Unlike LAN, MAN, and WAN, SAN is primarily defined by purpose rather than geographic size.
sections.callout: Servers need dedicated access to centralized storage → SAN.

sections.title: SAN vs. LAN
sections.callout: LAN = users and devices; SAN = storage.

sections.title: Wireless Local Area Network (WLAN)
paragraphs: A Wireless Local Area Network (WLAN) is a LAN using wireless technology such as Wi-Fi for client connectivity. It supports laptops, phones, tablets, and wireless printers without Ethernet to every endpoint.
sections.callout: Office users connect locally through Wi-Fi → WLAN.

sections.title: LAN vs. WLAN
paragraphs: Both describe local networks. LAN is the general local-network category; WLAN specifically emphasizes wireless local connectivity. A real site can include both wired LAN and WLAN access.
sections.callout: WLAN = LAN with wireless client connections.

sections.title: PAN vs. WLAN

table.caption: Wireless personal and local networks
rows: Very short-range network around one person
Wireless local network covering a home, office, or site

sections.callout: Phone to earbuds → PAN; laptop to office Wi-Fi → WLAN.

sections.title: Internet Connection vs. Network Type
paragraphs: An internet connection type describes how service reaches the customer. A network type classifies the customer's network by scale, method, or purpose.
A home can use fiber internet and a WLAN internally. A company can use cable internet, a LAN in each office, a WAN between offices, and a SAN for server storage.
sections.callout: Internet type = how the ISP reaches me; network type = what kind of network this is.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Fixed wireless connection to ISP tower → WISP
Network inside a home or office → LAN
Network around one person's devices → PAN
Network across a metropolitan area → MAN

sections.title: Objective 2.7 Exam Trap
paragraphs: First decide whether the question asks about internet delivery or network classification. Then use the medium, geographic scale, or specialized purpose.

entries.title: Satellite vs. WISP
paragraphs: A dish or terminal communicating with space points to satellite; a fixed receiver aimed at a terrestrial ISP tower points to WISP.

entries.title: Cellular vs. WISP
paragraphs: A mobile carrier points to cellular; a fixed wireless ISP points to WISP.

entries.title: Fiber vs. Cable vs. DSL
paragraphs: Optical fiber → fiber; coax → cable; telephone copper → DSL.

entries.title: LAN vs. WLAN
paragraphs: LAN is a general local network; WLAN specifically emphasizes wireless local connectivity.

entries.title: PAN vs. WLAN
paragraphs: One person's nearby devices → PAN; wireless network covering a local place → WLAN.

entries.title: MAN vs. WAN
paragraphs: City scope → MAN; broader distant networks → WAN.

entries.title: SAN vs. WAN
paragraphs: SAN describes storage purpose; WAN describes wide geographic scope.

sections.callout: HOW INTERNET ARRIVES or WHAT KIND OF NETWORK?

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Network type = geographic size, specialized purpose, or connection style
